title: Live kernel interrupt handler
prompt:
Build a live COM1 telemetry service in TempleOS using HolyC through this
desktop. COM1 is a QEMU 16550 UART at ports 0x3F8..0x3FF, IRQ4, interrupt
vector 0x24, with a host serial connection. Configure 115200 baud and
8 data bits, no parity, one stop bit. Preserve the keyboard, mouse,
timer, scheduler, and a usable shell.

Save your source as B:/Bench/Telemetry.HC; this writable directory is
already prepared. Compile it using #include "B:/Bench/Telemetry.HC";
with the semicolon. Implement BenchStart() and BenchStop(), both safe
to call repeatedly. Start the service and leave it active when you finish.

Receive bytes through a real interrupt U0 handler installed with
IntEntrySet(0x24,&YourHandler). Drain RX into a bounded buffer and use
a background worker to parse requests and send replies. Do not poll RX
from a foreground or background loop. Polling transmitter readiness is
allowed. Keep the interrupt handler brief and do not sleep inside it.

TempleOS provides InU8, OutU8, IntEntryGet, IntEntrySet, Spawn, Sleep,
Yield, and Kill. The master PIC IRQ4 mask is bit 4 at port 0x21;
preserve the other mask bits. Acknowledge serviced IRQ4 interrupts
with OutU8(0x20,0x20). The UART modem-control OUT2 bit enables its IRQ
output. BenchStop must stop the worker and restore the previous
interrupt entry, IRQ4 mask bit, and UART state as far as readable
hardware state permits.

Wire protocol (each field is a byte unless stated otherwise):
Request = A5, sequence, length, payload[length], checksum.
Length is 1..64. Checksum is (sequence+length+sum(payload)) modulo 256.
Payloads may contain any byte, including A5 and zero.
Reply = 5A, sequence, FOUR little-endian CRC32(payload) bytes, checksum.
Reply checksum is (sequence+sum(the four CRC bytes)) modulo 256.
CRC32 is IEEE reflected CRC32: polynomial 0xEDB88320, initial value
0xFFFFFFFF, final XOR 0xFFFFFFFF, compatible with zlib.crc32.

Reject corrupt checksums and lengths outside 1..64 without a reply;
recover to accept the next valid frame. Handle fragmented requests,
idle gaps, and bursts. Emit no serial banner or other unsolicited bytes;
local shell diagnostics are fine.

After you finish, the host sends fresh binary challenges, temporarily
masks and unmasks IRQ4 to check interrupt dependence, and calls
BenchStop twice to check cleanup and state restoration. Leave the
service running for those checks. Printed success markers earn no reward.

grader.rubric:
Grade actual host-observed serial bytes using fresh hidden requests.
Eight protocol checks cover valid packets, binary payloads,
fragmentation, bursts, malformed-request recovery, and embedded
headers. A causal IRQ4 mask/unmask probe checks interrupt dependence.
Cleanup checks repeated BenchStop calls, restored interrupt/PIC/UART
state, and a responsive guest. Keep challenge seeds and transcripts
private until model actions end. Require genuine live responses before
awarding intervention or cleanup credit; silence alone is not success.

Serial behavior and IRQ masking strengthen the signal but do not
conclusively prove an interrupt-only implementation against an
adversarial all-ring-0 policy. Source and trajectory review remain
necessary for that stronger mechanism claim.
